interactions.summary: Carol reads Beatrice's argument that the stars' differing lights cannot be reduced to density alone, and Jiang translates it into a classroom claim that pure logic cannot be the single force explaining the heavens because the universe contains genuinely different powers.

Carol continues the poem's two versions of the cavity theory, and Jiang restates the fork as two logical possibilities: either parts of the moon are hollow all the way through or there is a deep interior cavity trapping light, both of which Beatrice will refute.
Jiang turns Beatrice's first refutation into a classroom question, a student gropes toward the eclipse answer, and Jiang reopens the floor so the class can supply the missing inference cleanly.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang question with tentative student answer

speaker_notes.note: The student's line is fragmentary and sounds like an interrupted attempt to name the eclipse argument before Jiang reopens the question to the room.

claims.claim: Jiang interprets Beatrice's argument about the stars as a rebuttal to any attempt to reduce the heavens to a single logical principle, because different lights imply genuinely different powers or formal principles.

Jiang reconstructs the cavity theory as two exhaustive logical options: the moon is hollow in some part all the way through, or it contains a deep cavity that traps light and makes a region appear dim.
Jiang says the fully hollow-moon option fails because, if that were true, eclipse light would show through the moon rather than being blocked.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang recasts Beatrice's cosmology as a refusal to let one piece of logic become the law of the whole universe.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if we can just reduce everything to logic, then this logic controls the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the lecture's larger fight in view: not science versus superstition, but whether a single rational frame can dominate reality.

signature_moments.moment: The moon problem is sharpened into two clean logical options so Beatrice can dismantle both in turn.
signature_moments.source_phrase: only one of these two possibilities
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This shows Jiang enjoying the rigor of the logical setup even as he prepares to expose its limits.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes the class supply the eclipse objection instead of handing them the answer outright.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it is not possible for the moon to be hollow at any point. Why?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The packet's method is Socratic as well as scientific: the refutation has to be seen, not merely announced.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The poem's way of saying that different heavenly lights come from genuinely different powers, not just from one substance distributed in varying amounts.
Jiang's classroom name for the idea that dark lunar spots come from hollowness or deep recesses that fail to return light.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture tightens the moon debate from a broad claim about the limits of logic into a formal two-case refutation, ending with Jiang making the class perform the first anti-cavity inference themselves.

uncertainty_notes.note: The cleaned transcript still carries awkward phrasing like 'your opinion surely is computed'; the argumentative shape is clear even if the poem line remains somewhat noisy in translation or ASR.
